native_comparison.bound_statement: For every captured row (picked token t) the bound reported here is: |native_logprob - transformers_bf16_logprob| <= native_vs_fp64_box + tf_bf16_vs_fp64_box + |(x_bf16 - x_native) @ W_t| + max_v |(x_bf16 - x_native) @ W_v| + rounding_slack. The two boxes are the same boxed FP64 formulas recorded in the FP64 reference (gamma-series head bound with accumulation depth ceil(H/2048)*8+13, row-max head bound, logsumexp/reduction bound with depth ceil(V/256)+8, and the final FP32 subtraction rounding); they are recomputed here for each arm's own float32 logits. The two hidden-distance terms are the float64 lm_head product of the difference between the transformers BF16 normalized hidden row and the native captured one; they bridge the fact that the two arms are not evaluated on identical hidden states. All 18 rows satisfy this bound (max ratio 0.169451).
native_comparison.capture_mapping_statement: Captured rows are mapped to fixture positions by the capture tool's own rule, not by a nearest-hidden search. qwen35_score_reference.zig forwards each captured fixture as one prompt chunk and captures the last min(scored, 2) scored prompt rows, i.e. positions [L-2, L-1] (hidden rows [L-3, L-2]), followed by four one-row decode captures at positions [L+1, L+4] (hidden rows [L, L+3]). Every mapping here is verified by an exact match of the captured picks against ids[L-2:L] and against the four served greedy continuation tokens. The recorded hidden distances explain why a nearest search is not used: fixture 3 repeats its last two tokens at 16 positions and the two serves' BF16 hidden rows diverge there, so the nearest decoy can be far from the true row.
native_comparison.receipt_form_statement: The receipt-style decomposition |native - transformers_bf16| <= (native vs FP64 bound at the picked token) + (measured |transformers_bf16 - transformers_fp32| at the picked token) + rounding slack does NOT hold on 1 of 18 rows [13] (largest receipt-style ratio 3.00215). On those rows the native and transformers BF16 hidden trajectories have separated far enough (see hidden_l2_distance) that the native-vs-FP64 box alone no longer covers the distance; it is a diagnostic decomposition whose middle term is a measured difference, not a bound, so the rigorous two-box-plus-hidden-distance statement above is the valid one. Separately, the measured BF16-vs-FP32 logprob difference is itself within its own boxed bound on all rows (max delta-bound ratio 0.999354).

first_row_logits_compare.note: library logits are the BF16 module output; the reported logprobs use the float32 GEMM path

fp32.upcast_semantics: per-layer streaming promotion: each decoder layer's stored BF16 parameters/buffers are promoted to float32, the layer runs, then the stored BF16 values are restored before the next layer; the final norm is promoted the same way and the BF16-stored lm_head is promoted to float32 for the scoring matmul. BF16->FP32 promotion is exact, so this is float32 arithmetic over the checkpoint's stored values -- it is NOT a trained float32 checkpoint and no claim of exact fp32-partial sums is made for any single fused kernel.
fp32.params_resident_fp32: one decoder layer at a time (peak transient ~0.8 GB)

bf16_dtype_head_vs_fp32_gemm.note: a BF16 head matmul returns BF16 logits; the reported logprobs use the float32 GEMM over the same promoted BF16-stored weights, so the delta between the two arms isolates activation/accumulation precision rather than logit storage

lm_head_promotion_vs_fp32_gemm.note: float32 linear over an explicitly promoted vocabulary chunk vs the chunked float32 GEMM path used for the reported logprobs; the full float32 lm_head copy is never materialized
